entities.name: Muhammad ibn Mahmud Amuli
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Muhammad ibn Mahmud al-Amuli (died 1352), a towering figure in 14th-century Persian intellectual life, epitomized the encyclopedic scholarship characteristic of the late Islamic Golden Age. Hailing from Amol in Tabaristan (modern Iran), Amuli was not merely a physician but a polymath whose monumental work, *Nafāʾis al-funūn fī ʿarāʾis al-ʿuyūn* (The Precious Sciences in the Brides of the Eyes), synthesized an astonishing breadth of knowledge across medicine, philosophy, astronomy, mathematics, and various other disciplines. His contributions provided a vital bridge, preserving and transmitting classical Islamic and Hellenistic sciences during a period of significant geopolitical upheaval following the Mongol invasions, ensuring continuity for future generations of scholars in the Ilkhanate and subsequent dynasties.

Amuli's magnum opus, *Nafāʾis al-funūn*, completed around 1339, stands as one of the most comprehensive encyclopedias of its era, comprising an astounding 150 sciences divided into two main sections: the traditional (religious, linguistic, literary) and the rational (philosophical, scientific, mathematical). Within the rational sciences, Amuli meticulously detailed subjects from logic and metaphysics to natural philosophy, medicine, and the occult sciences, often drawing upon and critically engaging with the works of predecessors like Ibn Sina (Avicenna) and Razi. His medical sections, in particular, offered detailed anatomical descriptions, pharmacological treatises, and clinical observations, reflecting centuries of accumulated Islamic medical knowledge.
